This script includes my data cleaning, condensed down, as well as testing and exploratory data analysis.

# Cleaning

For my project, I needed to combine two separate datasets and arrange them so that I had the information I needed from my simulation. For the quotas, I used data directly from the IMF (cite), and for information on loan conditions, I used data from an IMF monitor group (cite). I cleaned each separately, and then I merged them.

A quick note - changing column names seemed to sometimes make it so that nothing could render. If that happens, it's likely because I had to change it to the new column name so it would run again.

### Quota data

I started by setting up my library and reading in the raw data.

```{r}
#| message: false

# Library set-up

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(lubridate)
library(tinytable)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}

# Reading in the raw quota data

raw_quota_data <-
  read.csv("raw_quota_data.csv")

head(raw_quota_data)
```

Next, I needed to drop the columns that I didn't need, change the column names, get rid of empty rows, and make sure all the country names made sense. I also needed to arrange it alphabetically so it would be easier to merge with my other data down the line.

```{r}

# Dropping columns

quota_data <- 
  select(raw_quota_data, 1, 2)

# Dropping empty rows

quota_data <- quota_data %>%
  slice(3:195) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(trimws(.), ""))) %>%
  remove_empty("rows")

# Renaming columns

quota_data <-
  rename(quota_data,
         country_name = Table.1..Updated.Quota.Formula.Variables.Shares.1.,
         quota_percent = X)

# Arranging alphabetically

quota_data <-
  arrange(quota_data, country_name)

# Changing "China 2/" to "China"

quota_data <-
  quota_data |>
  mutate(
    country_name = str_replace_all(country_name, "China 2/", "China")
  )

head(quota_data)
```

Once I had the cleaned quota data, I moved on to the conditionality data.

### Conditionality data

The conditionality data was nicer in that it was used for research, and was thus formatted properly. However, it was a lot further from what I actually needed for my final dataset, so there was a bit more cleaning to do. To start, I had to read in the raw data.

```{r}

# Reading in raw conditionality data

raw_conditionality_data <-
  read.csv("raw_IMF_conditionality_data.csv")

head(raw_conditionality_data)
```

Next, I had to remove the columns I didn't need.

```{r}

# Removing columns I don't need

messy_conditionality_data <-
  select(raw_conditionality_data, 1, 8, 13)

head(messy_conditionality_data)
```

Then, the issue was that each loan was it's own row. But what I wanted was country-level information with total number of loans, total number of each condition type, and total number of each condition policy area. First, I started with counting the total number of each loan for each country by counting how many times each country shows up.

```{r}

# Counting total number of conditions

total_conditionality <-
  count(messy_conditionality_data,
        Country.Name)

head(total_conditionality)
```

Then, I wanted to count the number of each type of condition and each policy area, which ended up being more complicated than I expected, but worked out in the end.

```{r}

# Counting the number of each condition type

df_type_original <- 
  table(messy_conditionality_data$Country.Name,
        messy_conditionality_data$Condition.Type)

head(df_type_original)

# Counting the number of each policy area

df_policy_area_original <- 
  table(messy_conditionality_data$Country.Name,
        messy_conditionality_data$Condition.Policy.Area)

head(df_policy_area_original)
```

The next thing I had to do was make the three data frames into tibble form so that I could more easily change the column names, and merge them eventually.

```{r}

# Changing into tibble format

df_type <- 
  as_tibble(as.data.frame.matrix(df_type_original), rownames = "country_name")

head(df_type)

df_policy_area <- 
  as_tibble(as.data.frame.matrix(df_policy_area_original), 
            rownames = "country_name")

head(df_policy_area)

total_conditionality <-
  as_tibble(total_conditionality)

head(total_conditionality)
```

```{r}

# Changing column names

total_conditionality <-
  rename(total_conditionality,
         country_name = Country.Name,
         total_conditions = n) 

head(total_conditionality)

df_type <-
  rename(df_type,
         type_IB = IB,
         type_PA = PA,
         type_PC = PC,
         type_QPC = QPC,
         type_SB = SB,
         type_SPC = SPC)

head(df_type)

df_policy_area <-
  rename(df_policy_area,
         area_DEB = DEB,
         area_ENV = ENV,
         area_EXT = EXT,
         area_FIN = FIN,
         area_FP = FP,
         area_INS = INS,
         area_LAB = LAB,
         area_OTH = OTH,
         area_POV = POV,
         area_PRI = PRI,
         area_RTP = RTP,
         area_SOE = SOE,
         area_SP = SP)

head(df_policy_area)
```

Just a note – once I changed one column name, I had to use the new one every time, so there's so confusion in how it looks. But it's just because of this, and I found that commenting out as I went tended to help with this issue!

### Merging

The last step was to merge my different data frames. This ended up being a lot easier than I thought! First, I merged my conditionality data frames. Then, I got rid of the extra columns with the country name. Then, I merged those on to my quota data.

```{r}

# Merging my conditionality data

merged_conditionality <-
  bind_cols(total_conditionality, df_type, df_policy_area)

# Getting rid of repeated country_name columns

merged_conditionality <-
  select(merged_conditionality, 1:2, 4:9, 11:23)

# Changing the country_name column

merged_conditionality <-
  rename(merged_conditionality,
         country_name = "country_name...1")

head(merged_conditionality)
```

```{r}

# Merging with my quota data

test_merge <- quota_data %>%
  left_join(merged_conditionality, by = "country_name")

# Changing "NA" to 0

test_merge[is.na(test_merge)] <- 0

# Renaming the data frame

df_final <- test_merge

head(df_final)
```

That leaves me with my cleaned data, called df_final.

# Tests

The first thing I noticed before even testing was that my quota_percent column was in character form (chr), when I need it to be a numeric (dbl). Also, all my conditions and policy area columns are in numeric form (dbl), which kind of makes sense, but in reality, it needs to be an integer, since there can't be decimals in the number of loans. So, I'll change that:

```{r}

# Changing the quota_percent column from <chr> to <dbl>

df_final$quota_percent <- as.numeric(df_final$quota_percent)

# Changing the conditions and policy area columns from <dbl> to <int>

df_final <- df_final %>%
  mutate(across(c(total_conditions, 
                  type_IB, 
                  type_PA, 
                  type_PC, 
                  type_QPC, 
                  type_SB, 
                  type_SPC, 
                  area_DEB, 
                  area_ENV, 
                  area_EXT, 
                  area_FIN, 
                  area_FP, 
                  area_INS, 
                  area_LAB, 
                  area_OTH, 
                  area_POV, 
                  area_PRI, 
                  area_RTP, 
                  area_SOE, 
                  area_SP), as.integer))

head(df_final)
```

Another thing I want to check is that quota_percent adds up to 100, since they should add up to 100% of the quota between all countries. This isn't as simple as I hoped, because of tiny differences in decimals, so instead of checking if it added to 100, I just checked the sum. It's off by 0.0024%, which isn't nothing, but is probably due to rounding errors. While it might not technically pass the test fully, it passes for what I actually need to do.

```{r}

# Testing if quota_percent adds up to 100

sum(df_final$quota_percent) == 100

# Checking what it actually adds to, to see if the difference actually matters

sum(df_final$quota_percent)
```

I also want to make sure that total_conditions is equal to both the total number of condition types and the total number of policy areas (separately).

```{r}

# Testing if total_conditions = the sum of all the condition types

sum(df_final[, 
             c("type_IB", 
               "type_PA", 
               "type_PC", 
               "type_QPC", 
               "type_SB", 
               "type_SPC")], 
    na.rm = TRUE) ==
      sum(df_final$total_conditions, na.rm = TRUE)

# Testing if total_conditions = the sum of all the policy areas

sum(df_final[, 
             c("area_DEB", 
               "area_ENV", 
               "area_EXT", 
               "area_FIN", 
               "area_FP", 
               "area_INS", 
               "area_LAB", 
               "area_OTH", 
               "area_POV", 
               "area_PRI", 
               "area_RTP", 
               "area_SOE", 
               "area_SP")], na.rm = TRUE) ==
  sum(df_final$total_conditions, na.rm = TRUE)

# Not true - going to check what went wrong

sum(df_final$total_conditions)

sum(df_final[, 
             c("area_DEB", 
               "area_ENV", 
               "area_EXT", 
               "area_FIN", 
               "area_FP", 
               "area_INS", 
               "area_LAB", 
               "area_OTH", 
               "area_POV", 
               "area_PRI", 
               "area_RTP", 
               "area_SOE", 
               "area_SP")])
```

By doing that last test, I realized I made a mistake earlier when I merged my columns. After I go back and fix that, that test should come back as true. What happened was that I missed the last few columns when getting rid of the repeated country name column when merging, so it didn't make it to my final dataset. I added them into the merge and back into the tests, which now show as true.

# Graphs

There are a lot of different ways to visualize this dataset. When I first started the project, I had wanted to look at how quota percentage (which is directly related to voting power) is correlated with total number of conditions. I'm going to try first to make a scatter plot showing the correlation between quota percent and total number of conditions. I made the scale on the x-axis very small, because the vast majority of countries only have a very small quota, and those are the countries that tend to also have loans.

```{r}

# Making a scatter plot of quota percent and total number of conditions
# Only one country is above 15% quota, so removing that from the scale
# Also, countries with loans usually have even lower quotas, so I make smaller

df_final |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = quota_percent, y = total_conditions)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.4, colour = "seagreen4") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Number of Loan Conditions and IMF Quota",
    x = "IMF Quota (Percent)",
    y = "Total Number of Conditions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    element_text(family = "sans")
  )
  
```

This is good, and does match the relationship I expected, where lower quota percent is correlated with a higher number of loans.

I also want to see whether there is any trend regarding the type of condition and the quota percent. To do this, I'm going to make a scatter plot where that is differentiated by colour. I used a jitter plot so the groupings between variables was more obvious, but I had to change the width manually since my scale was so small.

```{r}

# By condition 

ggplot(df_final, aes(x = quota_percent)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_IB, color = "IB"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_PA, color = "PA"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_PC, color = "PC"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 1, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_QPC, color = "QPC"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_SB, color = "SB"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_SPC, color = "SPC"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    y = "Total Number of Conditions", 
    x = "IMF Quota (Percent)", 
    color = "Condition Type",
    title = "Number of Conditions by Type and IMF Quota") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = "sans")
  )
```

This way, we can see that certain types of conditions group together in different areas. For example, we see that yellow dots, referring to SPC type, are concentrated along the x-axis, meaning that many countries do not have this type of condition (because total number of conditions is zero). At the same time, we can see that a number of countries with low IMF quotas do have this type of condition. While I'm not yet able to make the graph interactive, by changing the transparency of different variables, I can also see where variables are concentrated. For example, when I make PC (green) less transparent, I can see that it is also concentrated along the x-axis, but unlike SPC, is not as common in general.

While there does seem to be a second clump of values around 2% quota, the majority are under 1%. We can change the scale of the x-axis again to only go to 1, we can see more detail.

```{r}

# Making the x-axis smaller

ggplot(df_final, aes(x = quota_percent)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_IB, color = "IB"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_PA, color = "PA"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_PC, color = "PC"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 1, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_QPC, color = "QPC"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_SB, color = "SB"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_SPC, color = "SPC"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    y = "Total Number of Conditions", 
    x = "IMF Quota (Percent)", 
    color = "Condition Type",
    title = "Number of Conditions by Type and IMF Quota") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = "sans")
  )
```

Another type of graph I could make is essentially the same, but with fewer colours that represent whether condition types are binding or not binding. QPC, PA, SPC, and PC conditions are binding, meaning countries are required to meet them. IB and SB are non-binding, intended as goals.

```{r}

ggplot(df_final, aes(x = quota_percent)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_IB, color = "Non-binding"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_PA, color = "Binding"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_PC, color = "Binding"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 1, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_QPC, color = "Binding"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_SB, color = "Non-binding"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = type_SPC, color = "Binding"), 
              size = 2.5, alpha = 0.3, width = 0.1, height = 0.3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    y = "Total Number of Conditions", 
    x = "IMF Quota (Percent)", 
    color = "Condition Type",
    title = "Number of Conditions by Type and IMF Quota") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = "sans")
  )
```

This shows us that binding conditions are less common, because they are concentrated along the x-axis. However, it is also notable that non-binding conditions are common, especially for countries with lower quotas.

We could also make a bar plot of the most common condition types and policy areas.

```{r}

# Finding the totals for each type of condition

type_totals <-
  colSums(df_final[, c("type_IB", 
                       "type_PA", 
                       "type_PC", 
                       "type_QPC", 
                       "type_SB", 
                       "type_SPC")])

type_totals

# Finding the totals for each policy area

area_totals <-
  colSums(df_final[, c("area_DEB", 
                       "area_ENV", 
                       "area_EXT", 
                       "area_FIN", 
                       "area_FP", 
                       "area_INS", 
                       "area_LAB", 
                       "area_OTH", 
                       "area_POV", 
                       "area_PRI", 
                       "area_RTP", 
                       "area_SOE", 
                       "area_SP")])

area_totals

# Making a bar plot of condition type

type_totals %>%
  enframe(name = "type", value = "count") %>%
  mutate(type = str_remove(type, "type_")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(type, -count), y = count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "maroon") +
  labs(title = "Totals by Condition Type", 
       x = "Condition Type", 
       y = "Number of Conditions") +
  theme_minimal()

area_totals %>%
  enframe(name = "area", value = "count") %>%
  mutate(area = str_remove(area, "area_")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(area, -count), y = count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "orange2") +
  labs(title = "Totals by Policy Area", 
       x = "Policy Area", 
       y = "Number of Conditions") +
  theme_minimal()

```

This shows us that QPC (Quantitative Performance Criteria) is the most common condition type, followed closely by SB (Structural Benchmarks). QPC is binding, and SB is not. By far, the least common condition type is PC (Performance Criteria). This type of condition is included no matter what, so if any other conditions get added, it's coded as the higher-level condition, which then makes sense why there are so few.

For policy area, we can see that FIN (Financial Sector, Monetary Policy, and Central Bank) is the most common, which makes sense because we're talking about IMF loans. That's followed quite closely by DEB (External Debt) and FP (Fiscal Policy). The least common policy areas are ENV (Land and Environment), OTH (Other: residual category), and SP (Social Policy: Restrictive or Neutral).

# Conclusion

There weren't many things that I found super surprising, because the correlation I'm looking at is pretty obvious; of course countries with lower quota tend to have more loan conditions, because they are poorer countries who probably need more loans. One thing I did find interesting was that there were more binding conditions than non-binding conditions. I had expected to see more non-binding conditions, because those are easier to make. In terms of data visualization specifically, it occurred to me that the way I had imagined representing my data – as a scatter plot – might be confusing in some ways. The way I set it up – with the y-axis showing number of conditions – made it seem like there were a ton of loans of one type concentrated in one area. In reality, that means that there were fewer loans of that type, since they are grouping near the x-axis at 0. But at first glance, it looks very different! This made me think about how visualization is important.
